overview.text: Vasco da Gama commanded a Portuguese fleet that sailed from Lisbon in 1497, rounded southern Africa, and reached Calicut on India’s southwest coast in 1498. His was the first recorded European sea voyage linking Europe directly to India by that route, but Indian Ocean merchants and sailors already knew and used its waters. King Manuel I sought trade and diplomatic ties with Calicut’s ruler, the Zamorin. The difficult expedition returned in 1499 and opened a new phase of Portuguese activity in the Indian Ocean. Da Gama later led another voyage to India, became Count of Vidigueira, and died at Cochin in 1524.

Da Gama became Count of Vidigueira in 1519.
He was named viceroy in 1524 and died at Cochin that year.

overview.text: Shaka kaSenzangakhona led the Zulu kingdom in southeastern Africa during the early nineteenth century. Rising to power around 1816, he expanded the kingdom through conquest, diplomacy, and the incorporation of neighboring communities. He strengthened age-based regiments called amabutho and is closely associated with close-combat spears and the “chest and horns” encircling tactic. Some weapons and practices attributed to him existed earlier, so claims that he invented every reform are uncertain. His expansion formed part of the wider upheaval often called the Mfecane or Difaqane. Historians debate its causes, including earlier regional rivalries and colonial pressures. Shaka was assassinated in 1828; his half-brother Dingane succeeded him.

overview.text: Venezuela lies on the Caribbean coast of northern South America. Its landscape includes the Lake Maracaibo basin in the northwest, the broad Llanos plains, and the Orinoco River basin. Petroleum has long shaped its economy and politics, especially around Maracaibo and the Orinoco region. In 1960, President Rómulo Betancourt survived a car-bomb assassination attempt linked by contemporary investigations to Dominican dictator Rafael Trujillo. Venezuela took the case to the Organization of American States, making it a regional diplomatic crisis. Its diplomatic response also shows how a national political crisis could become an international dispute during the Cold War.

Lake Maracaibo lies in its northwestern basin.
Petroleum has been central to the Venezuelan economy.

overview.text: Philip II ruled Spain from 1556 to 1598 during a period of Habsburg power and intense European religious conflict. Before inheriting the Spanish crown, he married England’s Queen Mary I in 1554, a union unpopular with many of her subjects. Mary died without an heir in 1558, and her half-sister Elizabeth I became queen. Relations between Philip and Elizabeth eventually turned hostile. Philip sent the Spanish Armada in 1588 as part of a planned invasion of England, but the fleet failed to secure a crossing for troops from the Netherlands. His reign is a useful anchor for studying the Catholic Reformation, Anglo-Spanish rivalry, and the limits of early modern naval power.

overview.text: Philip IV reigned as Habsburg king of Spain from 1621 to 1665, a period marked by costly European wars and political strains within the Spanish monarchy. Spain fought in the Thirty Years’ War, and conflicts with France continued to challenge its power. Philip is also remembered as a major patron of the arts. Diego Velázquez became his court painter in 1623 and produced many portraits of the king. In Velázquez’s 1656 painting Las Meninas, Philip and Queen Mariana appear reflected in a mirror while their daughter, the infanta Margarita, stands among attendants. The work connects Philip’s court, family, and the art of Spain’s Golden Age.

overview.text: Henry Knox began the American Revolution as a Boston bookseller with a strong interest in military history. George Washington entrusted him with moving captured heavy guns from Fort Ticonderoga to the Continental Army outside Boston during the winter of 1775–76. The artillery helped the Americans fortify Dorchester Heights and contributed to the British evacuation of Boston. Knox became chief of the Continental Army’s artillery and served at major campaigns, including Yorktown. After the war, he was Secretary of War under the Articles of Confederation and then the first person to hold that office in Washington’s federal cabinet, from 1789 to 1794. His career links Revolutionary battlefield logistics to the creation of the new government.

overview.text: The United Arab Emirates is a federation of seven emirates on the Arabian Peninsula, with coasts on the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman. Abu Dhabi is the federal capital; Dubai is another major city and the site of the Burj Khalifa. Six emirates formed the country in December 1971 after the end of British treaty arrangements, and Ras Al Khaimah joined in 1972. The seven members are Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Sharjah, Ajman, Umm Al Quwain, Ras Al Khaimah, and Fujairah. Its federal structure matters: each emirate has its own ruler and local government alongside national institutions. The country’s location has long tied it to maritime trade.

overview.text: The Cherokee people built and maintained political and cultural institutions in their southeastern homelands despite growing pressure from the United States and surrounding states. Sequoyah developed a Cherokee syllabary, enabling widespread reading and a bilingual newspaper, the Cherokee Phoenix. In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), the U.S. Supreme Court held that Georgia law had no force within Cherokee territory, but officials did not enforce the decision. A small faction signed the 1835 Treaty of New Echota without authorization from the Cherokee Nation’s government; Principal Chief John Ross and many citizens opposed it. U.S. forces expelled thousands in 1838–39 on the Trail of Tears. Cherokee nations and communities continue today.

overview.text: On June 28, 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie were assassinated in Sarajevo, then part of Austria-Hungary. Gavrilo Princip, a South Slav nationalist, fired the fatal shots. The killings triggered a diplomatic crisis: Austria-Hungary, with German support, delivered an ultimatum to Serbia and declared war on July 28. Russia backed Serbia, while Germany’s declarations against Russia and France and its invasion of Belgium widened the fighting. Within weeks, Europe was at war. The assassination was the immediate spark, but it did not alone make world war inevitable; alliance commitments, military plans, and preexisting tensions shaped the escalation.

overview.text: “Forty acres and a mule” became a memorable phrase for freedpeople’s hopes of land and economic independence after slavery. In January 1865, Union general William T. Sherman issued Special Field Orders No. 15, reserving coastal land from South Carolina to Florida for settlement by formerly enslaved people. It allowed family plots of up to forty acres; the written order did not itself promise a mule, though military animals were sometimes later provided. Black families began farming some of the land. After the Civil War, President Andrew Johnson’s policies returned much of it to former Confederate owners. The unfulfilled land program became a lasting symbol in debates over Reconstruction and reparations.

It specified family plots of no more than forty acres.

Johnson-era policy reversed much of the land distribution.
